items.title: Prior Straits
items.summary_raw: This is Heatmap Daily, a weekday news digest written by our executive editor. Sign up to receive it. For the first decade of my professional career, the U.S. economy was defined largely by its deficiencies. Employment lagged for years after the Great Recession, especially for non-college-educated men in their prime earning years. Money was free or cheap to borrow. Even after the housing market had recovered, economic activity remained moribund. Americans hated it, and politicians proposed various schemes to backfill the gap. One of these ideas was the Green New Deal — a once-in-a-generation investment in clean energy and low-carbon infrastructure that would put Americans back to work and deploy the economy’s spare capacity for the public good. How things have changed: The main story of the American economy today is one of constraints. On Tuesday, yields on 30-year Treasury bonds reached their highest level since 2002, meaning the federal government’s long-term borrowing costs are higher than they’ve been at any point since I was in elementary school. Electricity demand is surging, and global stockpiles of gasoline, diesel fuel, and crude oil are in short supply. No wonder, then, that many of the inputs to the energy system — such as transformers or natural gas turbines — remain expensive or in short supply. Or that the inflation rate remains stuck higher than 3%. What’s funny is that Americans still hate it. Consumer confidence fell last month to its lowest level since 2014…

items.title: Nuclear Energy for Sustainable Power Systems: An Integrated Assessment Using Life Cycle and Multi-Criteria Decision Approaches
items.summary_raw: The transition toward secure, low-carbon electricity generation requires energy technologies to be evaluated simultaneously in terms of environmental performance, technical reliability, economic viability, resource requirements, and strategic value. Although nuclear power is widely recognized as a low-carbon and high-capacity-factor technology, its overall benefits remain sensitive to fuel-cycle characteristics, system boundaries, economic assumptions, and decision criteria. This study presents a transparent literature-based comparative assessment of nuclear power using an integrated life-cycle assessment (LCA) and multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) framework. The environmental assessment was performed on a cradle-to-grave basis using 1 kWh of net electricity as the functional unit, while the MCDA incorporated 14 technical, environmental, economic, resource, and strategic indicators. Min–max normalisation and equal baseline weighting were applied, followed by a ±20% weight-perturbation analysis over 130 simulations to examine ranking robustness. Literature-derived median life-cycle greenhouse-gas emissions were approximately 12 g CO₂-eq/kWh for nuclear, compared with 11, 48, 490 and 820 g CO₂-eq/kWh for wind, solar photovoltaic, natural gas and coal, respectively. The resulting MCDA scores were 0.746 for nuclear, 0.706 for wind, 0.643 for solar PV, 0.566 for natural gas, and 0.404 for coal. Nuclear retained the first position in 93.8% of sensitivity simulations…

items.title: Between rhetoric and reality: Governance of just transition in Portugal's coal phase-out
items.summary_raw: Portugal's 2021 coal phase-out was celebrated politically as a milestone of climate leadership. This article interrogates the governance of the process using a Just Transition framework, examining the relationships between policy commitments, institutional implementation, administrative outcomes and workers' experiences. Drawing on documentary analysis, fieldwork, and sixteen semi-structured interviews with directly employed workers, public officials and company representatives, we examine how just transition guidelines were framed in national policy and applied in the closures of the Sines and Pego thermoelectric power plants. Neither municipality registered a marked rise in unemployment following the closures. Nevertheless, interviewed workers reported income loss, less meaningful work and an erosion of professional and social identity. Governance responses were largely technocratic, privileging compensation and reskilling, while workers perceived territorial investment as delayed or insufficient. Despite their different designs, the institutional arrangements in both territories converged on the same recorded outcome by different routes: redeployment, early retirement, employment-service placements and income-support measures each determined whether covered workers appeared in the unemployment register at all. The comparison therefore suggests that administrative indicators are not wholly independent measures of policy outcomes but are partly shaped by the instruments…

items.title: Subjective social status and willingness to pay for green taxes
items.summary_raw: Carbon pricing and green taxes are considered the most effective fiscal tools in combating climate change from a neoclassical economic perspective. However, increasing global protests have shown that the societal acceptance of these policies is deeply tied to individuals' perceptions of fairness and equity, rather than rational cost–benefit analyses. The current literature tends to explain tax resistance primarily through low-income levels or a lack of environmental knowledge. The main objective of this study is to analyse tax resistance not merely as a problem of economic constraint, but through the lens of relative deprivation felt by individuals regarding their position in the social hierarchy and the breach of the social contract between them and the state. The study argues, as a theoretically motivated interpretation rather than a directly tested claim, that individuals who feel left behind in terms of social status may be more likely to frame green taxes not as an environmental protection policy, but as an unfair imposition by the system. The study uses the 2020 Environment IV module of the International Social Research Program. The dependent variable is individuals' Willingness to Pay. The main independent variable is Subjective Social Status (SSS), an indicator that measures where an individual positions themselves on the social hierarchy. The Ordered Probit Model was chosen as the analysis method due to the ordinal nature of the dependent variable. In the model; to…

items.title: Climate Change and Disaster Risk Reduction Frameworks: Challenges and Opportunities for Youth-Led Community Mobilization
items.summary_raw: Bangladesh is one of the most climate vulnerable countries in the world, with its coastal regions severely affected by climate-related extremes. This paper identifies existing provisions for youth involvement in disaster risk reduction (DRR) frameworks and examines the opportunities and practical challenges they face in community mobilization. In method, efforts were made to extract all youth-related narratives from relevant literature. A total of 100 youth volunteers were surveyed, and in-depth interviews were conducted with six experts from youth-led organizations and four youth volunteers. The findings reveal that policy gaps, coordination difficulties, limited resources and recognition, non-inclusiveness, patriarchal attitudes, and bureaucratic red tape are major challenges encountered by youth volunteers. Notably, Bangladeshi youth demonstrate strong volunteerism, effective use of information technology, potential for capacity building, engagement with grassroots communities, and the ability to strengthen Union Disaster Management Committees (UDMCs), all of which can contribute to a sustainable community-based DRR approach. As rights-holders, youth empowerment is critically important. Relevant stakeholders—especially state actors, global leaders, forums, and funding organizations—should give greater attention to maximizing the contributions of youth in this field.

items.title: Optimizing Renewable Energy Utilization in the Manufacturing Industry in Indonesia
items.summary_raw: Background: Indonesia's manufacturing sector contributes substantially to global energy demand and greenhouse gas emissions, yet renewable energy accounts for only about 15% of industrial energy use. Although relevant policies are in place, food and beverage manufacturers continue to encounter technical, financial, and institutional barriers to integrating clean energy. Objective: This study aims to examine the associations of technical, economic, policy, and energy management factors with the optimization of renewable energy utilization in Indonesia's food and beverage manufacturing industry. Methods: This study employed a quantitative approach using multiple linear regression analysis. Data were collected through questionnaires distributed to 102 stakeholders in the food and beverage manufacturing industry who were selected using purposive sampling. The data were analyzed using validity and reliability tests, t-tests, an F-test, and the coefficient of determination (R²). Results: The results indicate that, collectively, technical, economic, policy, and energy management factors are significantly associated with renewable energy optimization (F = 577.237, p < 0.05). Individually, technical factors (t = 4.592, p < 0.05) and policy factors (t = 4.653, p < 0.05) show positive and significant associations, whereas economic and energy management factors do not show significant associations. The R² value of 0.958 suggests that the model explains a substantial proportion of the…

items.title: From artificial intelligence to renewable energy transition: pathways through green innovation and institutional readiness
items.summary_raw: As emerging economies seek to decarbonize energy systems and advance the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly SDG seven on affordable and clean energy, artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming a transformative capability, yet its contribution to the renewable energy transition remains insufficiently explained. This study examines how AI is associated with the renewable energy transition in 23 emerging economies from 2015 to 2023, with particular attention to the mechanisms and conditions that shape this relationship. It develops a conditional process framework in which green technological innovation (GTI) serves as the transmission mechanism, cybersecurity conditions the AI–GTI and AI–renewable energy transition relationships, together with environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance conditions the GTI–renewable energy transition pathway. Hayes’s PROCESS macro estimates direct, mediating, moderating, and conditional indirect effects, while two-step System GMM verifies the consistency of the PROCESS-based findings. The results show a positive indirect association between AI and renewable energy transition through GTI, while the direct association remains significant, indicating partial mediation. Cybersecurity strengthens the contribution of AI to both GTI and renewable energy transition; it also increases the indirect AI–GTI–renewable energy transition effect. ESG performance strengthens GTI’s contribution to the renewable energy transition and…

items.title: Stakeholders' Strategies and Channels of Climate Communication in the Bamenda Highlands, Cameroon
items.source_name: International Journal of Environment and Climate Change
items.summary_raw: This paper assesses the current communication strategies and channels used by different stakeholders in disseminating climate information in the Bamenda Highlands of Cameroon. The assessment goes beyond cataloguing what exists to examine whether the identified strategies and channels are capable of communicating climate variability and change information effectively. Climate variability and change information is understood here as scientifically grounded content on shifting rainfall patterns, temperature trends, increasing frequency of extreme weather events, and the consequences of these shifts for agricultural systems and community livelihoods. Drawing on a mixed-methods design that combined a stratified survey of 408 respondents, 30 key-informant interviews, eight focus-group discussions and 45 structured field observations across eight Sub-Divisions (Bamenda I–III, Kumbo Central, Nkambe Central, Santa, Oku and Fundong), the study maps participatory methods, media channels, institutional actors and communication frequency. Focus-group discussions dominate participatory approaches, yet function mainly as general environmental sensitisation rather than structured climate-science communication. Heat maps, a correlation matrix, labelled scatter plots and radar profiles of the eight Sub-Divisions show that regular programming co-varies with private weather services and independent media, that reactive communication is the statistical inverse of that cluster, and that mobile…

items.title: School Climate and Teachers’ Creativity in Tunisian Middle Schools
items.source_name: Journal of Educational Sciences – Qatar University
items.summary_raw: This study examines the relationship between school climate and teachers’ creativity in Tunisian middle schools. It draws on a random sample of 572 teachers from 44 preparatory schools and employs a mixed-methods design. In the quantitative phase, the researcher identified the preparatory school in Tunis Governorate that achieved the highest levels of teacher creativity. This was followed by an in-depth qualitative phase aimed at explaining how the school climate supports the group of teachers within that school. The findings indicate that the ‘relationships’ dimension represents the most influential factor in teachers’ creativity, followed by the ‘teaching and learning’ dimension. By contrast, the dimensions of ‘institutional environment’ and ‘safety’ demonstrated relatively lower effects. The qualitative phase also revealed an emergent dimension, namely ‘school culture,’ as a potentially supportive factor that enhances creative practices. Overall, the study provides a data-driven analytical account of how the dimensions of school climate interact with teachers’ creativity. It offers a structured framework for future research and a practical guide for efforts aimed at fostering creative practices in similar educational contexts.

items.title: Community radio as a catalyst for social learning, knowledge co-production, and adaptive capacity: a sequential explanatory mixed-methods study in Northern Ghana
items.summary_raw: Introduction Community radio has increasingly been recognised as an important platform for climate communication in sub-Saharan Africa. However, limited empirical evidence exists on how community radio contributes to social learning, climate knowledge co-production, and the adaptive capacity of smallholder farmers. This study examined the role of community radio in enhancing drought adaptation among smallholder farmers in Northern Ghana. Methods A mixed-methods approach was employed involving 1,200 smallholder farmers. Data were collected through household surveys and key informant interviews. Thematic analysis, descriptive statistics, and an Endogenous Switching Regression (ESR) model were used to analyse the data. Results The findings show that community radio strengthens social learning through information sharing, peer-to-peer learning, group discussions, observational learning, and leader-mediated diffusion. Community leaders, farmer groups, and informal social networks further amplified climate information obtained through radio programmes, extending its reach beyond direct listeners. Community radio also facilitated climate knowledge co-production by creating opportunities for collective interpretation, contextualisation, and validation of climate information through interactive formats such as call-in programmes, farmer testimonies, and community discussions. ESR estimates indicate that listening to community radio increased access to drought adaptation inputs and…

items.title: Biogas via Anaerobic Digestion: Innovations, Challenges for Sustainable Energy
items.summary_raw: Anaerobic digestion (AD) is a vital technology for sustainable waste management and renewable energy production, converting organic waste into methane-rich biogas and nutrient-rich digestate. Despite its potential, AD faces barriers to large-scale adoption, including feedstock variability, process instability, and high operational costs. This review critically evaluates recent advancements in AD technology, focusing on innovations that enhance efficiency and scalability, while identifying key challenges and policy gaps—particularly in developing economies. A systematic literature review (2014–2024) was conducted using PRISMA guidelines, analyzing 210 peer-reviewed studies from Scopus, Web of Science, and ScienceDirect. Quantitative and thematic analyses were performed using NVivo and VOSviewer. Recent advancements demonstrate that pretreatment strategies (e.g., enzymatic hydrolysis, thermal methods) improve biogas yields by 20–360%, while microbial bioaugmentation enhances process stability. Hybrid systems, such as temperature-phased AD, achieve 29% higher methane yields than conventional reactors, though economic viability remains dependent on policy support (e.g., the EU’s RED II incentives) and AI-driven optimization. Challenges persist in low-income regions due to high capital costs and infrastructural limitations. Future Directions: Integrating circular economy principles, hybrid renewable energy systems (e.g., AD-solar), and decentralized models can address scalability…

items.title: Government Policies and Renewable Energy Adoption: A Critical Review of Policy Instruments, Consumer Barriers and Administrative Challenges
items.source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.summary_raw: Abstract The transition from conventional energy sources to renewable energy has become an important part of national energy and sustainability strategies. Governments have introduced a range of measures, including subsidies, financial incentives, concessional finance, net-metering arrangements, feed-in mechanisms, renewable purchase obligations, awareness programmes and manufacturing support, to encourage renewable-energy adoption. However, the availability of policy support does not necessarily lead to widespread adoption. This paper critically reviews selected empirical and review studies concerning the relationship between government policies and renewable-energy adoption, with particular emphasis on solar photovoltaic and rooftop solar adoption in India. Ten relevant studies published between 2020 and 2024, together with supporting evidence from an earlier Indian study, are examined to identify recurring patterns in the literature. The review shows that high initial investment, limited access to finance, inadequate information, regulatory complexity, uncertainty about technology and maintenance, weak consumer confidence and differences in access to policy benefits continue to affect adoption. The literature also indicates that financial incentives are more likely to produce meaningful results when they are supported by simple application procedures, reliable information, appropriate grid arrangements, consumer protection and accessible financing. The review further…

items.title: Wpływ narracji klimatycznych w mediach na decyzje ekonomiczne: rola dezinformacji
items.summary_raw: The aim of this article is to examine how climate narratives in the media influence economic attitudes and the role that misinformation plays in this process, as it often shapes society’s perception of climate change. The analysis is based on both the literature on how climate change is presented and empirical material collected through a survey conducted among students at the University of Gdansk. The questionnaire consisted of ten closed-ended questions and focused primarily on sources of information about climate change, the level of trust in media messages, and the possible influence of those messages on economic attitudes. Additionally, a considerable share of respondents reported frequent exposure to climate-related content on social media, underscoring the growing importance of the digital information environment in shaping public opinion within the study group. The study involved 120 respondents. The results clearly show that the media strongly influence how climate change is perceived; however, this influence translates far less directly into respondents’ everyday economic decisions.

items.title: Harnessing Entrepreneurial Energy in Stakeholder Capitalism: A Quantitative Study of the Igbo Apprenticeship System
items.source_name: JOURNAL OF BUSINESS AND AFRICAN ECONOMY
items.summary_raw: The Igbo apprenticeship scheme (Igba Boi) is a culturally embedded informal training system that has historically underpinned entrepreneurship in southeastern Nigeria. This study investigates the scheme’s contemporary relevance, economic impact, and the institutional environment needed to sustain its contribution to Nigeria’s development. A mixed-methods approach combined a review of existing literature with a cross-sectional survey of 100 Igbo-origin entrepreneurs operating in ten major business hubs across all six geopolitical zones. A structured questionnaire measured perceptions of cultural significance, access to start-up capital, formalisation, and government policy support, alongside outcomes such as adoption, business survival, economic contribution, and job-creation/poverty-reduction effects. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Cronbach’s α, exploratory factor analysis, correlation, and multiple linear regression in EViews 13. Results indicate strong internal consistency of the measurement scales (α > 0.80) and a clear eight-factor structure aligning with the theoretical constructs. All independent variables—cultural significance (β = 0.36, p < 0.001), access to capital (β = 0.33, p < 0.001), formalisation (β = 0.35, p < 0.001), and policy support (β = 0.38, p < 0.001)—were positively and significantly associated with the respective outcomes (adoption/success, business survival, economic contribution, and job-creation/poverty reduction). The findings…

items.title: Recycled concrete aggregates in the circular economy: technological, environmental, and regulatory perspectives from Poland and Europe
items.source_name: Gospodarka Surowcami Mineralnymi - Mineral Resources Management
items.summary_raw: The construction sector is a major contributor to resource consumption and greenhouse gas emissions, requiring sustainable and circular material management. Recycled concrete aggregates (RCA) from construction and demolition waste are a key element of this transition. This study examines the development of the RCA market in Poland within EU circular economy policy, focusing on technology, regulation, and implementation barriers. A qualitative approach based on literature, regulatory analysis, and case studies was applied. The scope includes recycling technologies, RCA properties, water recovery systems, and a comparison of selected European countries. Results indicate that multi-stage processing enables high-quality RCA+ with properties comparable to natural aggregates. Up to 30% RCA does not significantly affect compressive strength, workability, or carbonation resistance. Pressure filtration systems allow water reuse without performance loss, while fine fraction utilization remains challenging. Despite progress, adoption in Poland is limited by variability, weak standardization, economic constraints, and low acceptance in structural applications. More advanced EU countries achieve higher recycling rates due to stronger regulatory and policy instruments. The study concludes that RCA supports decarbonization and resource efficiency in construction, but broader implementation requires technological improvement, regulatory alignment, and better-quality assurance. Future…

items.title: Sustainability and Willingness to Pay: A Review of Approaches in Urban Mobility and Climate Change Resilience
items.summary_raw: Willingness to pay (WTP) is widely used to inform sustainability-related policy and investment decisions, yet its application remains fragmented across research domains. In urban mobility, WTP is typically employed to value service quality improvements, technological adoption, and efficiency gains, while climate change resilience research primarily frames WTP around risk reduction, loss avoidance, and adaptation measures. These two domains are closely linked: transport systems contribute to environmental impacts and are highly vulnerable to climate disruption, so the value users place on mobility improvements depends on those services continuing to work when disruption occurs. Yet WTP studies in the two domains remain largely separate even though decarbonising transport and adapting it to climate risks both depend on public acceptance. This paper addresses this gap through a systematic literature review, which analyses how WTP is defined, measured, and applied, examining valuation logics, methodological approaches, valued attributes, and demographic and geographic coverage. The findings reveal heterogeneous conceptualisations of WTP, dominance of hypothetical valuation methods, and persistent gaps related to equity and cross-domain integration. By integrating these two bodies of research, this review develops a cross-domain taxonomy and proposes an analytical framework linking everyday mobility improvements with the maintenance and recovery of service benefits under climate…

items.title: Waste-to-Energy: A Bibliometric Analysis
items.summary_raw: This study presents a bibliometric analysis of waste-to-energy (WtE) research to map its intellectual structure, thematic evolution, influential works, and collaboration patterns. A total of 2,513 Scopus-indexed documents published between 2000 and 2026 were retrieved and analyzed with VOSviewer through keyword co-occurrence (network, overlay, and density visualizations), citation analysis, and co-authorship analysis at the author, institution, and country levels. The keyword network reveals five interconnected clusters: thermal conversion and plant energy performance, waste management systems and incineration residues, bioenergy and circular economy, technology selection and decision making, and life cycle and climate impacts. The overlay map shows a shift from boiler, heat recovery, and disposal-oriented studies toward renewable energy, anaerobic digestion, circular economy, life cycle assessment, and decision-support research, while the density map confirms that incineration-based WtE and waste management remain the dominant research core. The most cited documents are reviews on municipal solid waste management, circular economy, incineration, and food waste bioconversion. Co-authorship networks are organized into several cohesive but weakly connected groups, with Themelis as the most prominent author, and the United States, China, and India acting as the main country hubs, alongside a visible contribution from Indonesia and other emerging economies. The findings indicate…

items.title: What comes after social tipping? Perspectives from transitions towards net-zero
items.summary_raw: The world is on track to exceed 1.5 °C of warming. To avoid further temperature increase, accelerated action to decarbonize our societies is needed. Scholars claim that this transition requires surpassing social tipping points (STPs). STPs are defined as non-linear processes of transformative change in social systems, where a small perturbation triggers a response that generates self-amplifying changes in behaviors. While research efforts have focused on analyzing triggers to tipping, we have little understanding of the structures and mechanisms that stabilize a new state after the tipping phase. We argue that post-tipping trajectories rarely converge to a single stable state. Instead, they converge to multiple coexisting (including reversed) states that can exist as spatial patterns and need to be designed-in for stability. Combining insights from ecological systems, where phenomena that occur after tipping have been researched, with empirical evidence on social tipping in transitions towards net zero, we shed light on states after tipping and on how they may be stabilized. Four phenomena shape post-tipping trajectories: (i) lock-in through co-adoption of technologies or feedback loops; (ii) the co-existence of states; (iii) the reversibility of sustainable behaviors; and (iv) infrastructure as a stabilizer of co-existing or new states. We found that a systemic approach that combines technological and social levers to create positive feedback is needed to stabilize a future…

items.title: Solar Energy Adoption in Nepal’s Industrial Sector
items.summary_raw: Nepal’s industrial sector suffers from high energy consumption, high operating costs and unreliable grid supply, and industrial solar photovoltaics are developing as an alternative to diesel backup power generation. This study investigates the status, drivers and challenges for industrial solar uptake in Nepal by using publicly available sources, academic research publications, conference proceedings and international case studies. The solar capacity installed in Nepal has grown from 50 MW in 2019 to over 117 MW in 2024, with a further 27 grid-connected projects of 154.74 MW under development. Our illustrative techno-economic study found a system levelized cost of energy of approximately NPR 9.71/kWh for industrial rooftop solar, compared to approximately NPR 30/kWh for comparable capacity diesel generation, with typical installation costs ranging from NPR 85,000.00–100,000.00 per kWp. Industrial solar can replace diesel generation and reduce annual energy expenditures by 40–60%. Sensitivity analysis indicates that a 20% reduction in panel costs or a 10% increase in power tariffs can reduce payback periods by 1–1.5 years. Detailed Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats (SWOT) analysis identifies high upfront capital expenditures, legacy grid infrastructure, regulatory inconsistencies and institutional fragmentation as the major impediments. There are opportunities for international climate finance, smart-grid development and job creation. As Nepal-specific…

items.title: From volatility to viability: A stochastic evaluation of electricity-sourcing strategies and policy support for green hydrogen bankability in the Netherlands
items.summary_raw: Green hydrogen projects in the Netherlands face a critical bankability gap due to high costs and volatile energy markets. This study evaluates a 200-MW alkaline electrolyzer located in the Port of Rotterdam, the Netherlands, comparing three electricity-sourcing strategies: merchant market exposure, baseload green Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs), and hybrid renewable energy sources (RES)-integrated models. By integrating Monte Carlo price uncertainty with risk-adjusted project financing and expert insights, we show that without policy support, all base-case configurations are currently unbankable, with loss probabilities near 100% and mean levelized costs of hydrogen (LCOHs) spanning 6.94–8.67 €/kg H 2 (real, in 2024 values). However, hydrogen Contracts for Difference (CfDs) significantly improve project economics. Full de-risking through 15-year contracts establishes a 90% bankability frontier at strike prices of 6.67–7.34 €/kg H 2 for the RES-integrated configuration and 8.01–8.16 €/kg H 2 for the Baseload Green PPA configuration, substantially reducing downside risk relative to the unsupported baseline. In contrast, partial volume-constrained support remains insufficient to bridge the viability gap, leaving net present values negative. Within the scope of the evaluated configurations, the results suggest that revenue stabilization and downside risk mitigation are important determinants of bankability and may have a greater influence than marginal technical improvements…

items.title: How environmental media narratives shape the sustainability premium
items.source_name: Economics and Business Review/The Poznań University of Economics Review
items.summary_raw: This paper examines whether environmental narratives constitute an independent and state-dependent pricing channel in equity markets beyond conventional ESG scores and aggregate climate risk measures. Using more than 220 million US news articles, we construct indicators of environmental narrative sentiment and thematic intensity and analyse their effects on equal-weighted and value-weighted ESG portfolio premia. The empirical framework augments the Fama–French five-factor model with explicit climate risk and macroeconomic uncertainty controls and allows for delayed pricing effects. We find that environmental narratives, particularly attention-based measures, exert economically relevant effects on the equal-weighted sustainability premium, even after controlling for standard asset-pricing factors and climate-related risk indices, whereas the corresponding effects are substantially weaker in value-weighted portfolios. In contrast, aggregate ESG and climate risk measures display weak and unstable explanatory power once narratives are accounted for. The effects differ substantially across portfolio weighting schemes, while the lagged specifications provide more limited evidence of persistent delayed effects.

items.title: Governance Role Orientations, Perceived Governance Quality, and Citizen Participation in Climate Policy
items.summary_raw: ABSTRACT Climate change requires governance arrangements that coordinate governmental authority, civic action, and specialized contributions from nongovernmental actors. Yet research on climate‐policy participation has focused largely on formal participation opportunities, paying less attention to citizens' expectations regarding governance roles and their evaluations of policy processes. This study examines how three survey‐derived governance role orientations—governmental, civic, and industry‐and‐media orientations—and perceived climate policy governance quality are associated with two participation outcomes: institutional participation intention and climate‐related civic participation behavior. The analysis uses data from a nationwide quota‐based online survey of 500 adults in South Korea and applies hierarchical regression models. Civic orientation is positively associated with both participation outcomes, whereas governmental orientation is negatively associated with institutional participation intention. Industry‐and‐media orientation is not significantly associated with either outcome. Perceived climate policy governance quality is positively associated with both institutional participation intention and civic participation behavior, but none of its interactions with the three orientations is statistically significant. The findings distinguish citizens' expectations about governance roles from their evaluations of governance‐process quality. They suggest that civic…

items.title: Consumer attitudes toward millet and factors associated with its acceptance
items.source_name: The Journal of Almaty Technological University
items.summary_raw: Modern food systems face increasing pressure to support sustainable and healthy diets, which has renewed interest in nutrient-rich and climate-resilient crops such as millet. Despite its nutritional and functional potential, millet remains underutilised in contemporary diets. This study aimed to assess consumer awareness of and attitudes toward millet, willingness to incorporate it into the diet, and factors associated with its acceptance. A quantitative cross-sectional online survey was conducted among 270 respondents in Kazakhstan using a multilingual questionnaire in Kazakh, Russian, and English. The data were analysed using descriptive statistics. The results showed that 67.0% of respondents always checked product ingredients, indicating considerable attention to food composition, while more than 80% regularly consumed cereal products. At the same time, millet remained comparatively underutilised despite generally favourable attitudes toward it: more than 70% of respondents rated millet between 8 and 10 points. In addition, 61.1% preferred beverages containing fruit, cereal, or berry ingredients, suggesting openness to diversified product formulations. The findings reveal a gap between positive consumer attitudes toward millet and its actual integration into everyday diets. This suggests that nutritional awareness alone may not be sufficient to encourage regular consumption. Sensory appeal, product familiarity, direct tasting experience, clear product information, and…

items.title: Sparking change in residential electrification in Victoria: The role of local government
items.summary_raw: Decarbonising residential buildings is a central challenge in energy transitions and requires improving energy efficiency and shifting away from fossil fuels. How local governments can influence residential fuel choice without direct authority over energy markets and how their initiatives can shape subsequent higher-level regulation remain less understood. This paper examines Victoria, Australia, where long-standing fossil gas dependence rapidly shifted to all-electric residential development, culminating in a 2024 ban on new gas connections despite limited national leadership. The study draws on analysis of 27 policy documents and 26 semi-structured interviews with local and state government representatives, planners, developers, builders and advocacy organisations. Local governments reframed fossil gas as a climate and planning problem, using land-use policy to normalise all-electric housing. This demonstrated electrification's feasibility and helped enable subsequent state-level reform. The study identifies land-use planning as an indirect form of energy governance through which local governments can shape residential fuel choice despite lacking direct control over energy markets. It provides a planning-mediated account of how locally developed practices can contribute to wider energy-transition policy change.

items.title: Employment implications of liquid biofuels production in Ukraine under the climate neutrality goal by 2055
items.summary_raw: This article analyzes the potential impact of liquid biofuel production on employment in Ukraine within the context of pursuing climate neutrality by 2050. Despite progress in renewable electricity, the transport sector lags significantly behind the EU RED II and RED III Directive targets. The study assesses installed capacities against the 2030 National Renewable Energy Action Plan (2030 NREAP), identifies feasible biofuel types for sustainability and neutrality, and estimates employment effects using the employment factors method, with input from the TIMES-Ukraine model scenarios (WEM, WAM, NZE). Results indicate first-generation bioethanol dominance to 2030, shifting toward second-generation biofuels like biokerosene post-2030; employment could reach up to 46,000 jobs by 2055 (WAM) or 72,000 by 2045 (NZE), predominantly in feedstock supply, though outcomes depend on policy implementation, model assumptions (e.g., no exports), and external factors like war recovery. These projections highlight the potential for rural development amid uncertainties in global biofuel markets and domestic regulation.

items.title: Framing group sexual violence in the Italian press: newsworthiness, intersectionality, and the distortion of gender-based violence
items.summary_raw: While media representations play a decisive role in shaping public understanding of gender-based violence (GBV), newspaper reporting on group sexual assault remains an under-researched dimension. Situated within the STEP Observatory’s ongoing monitoring of the Italian press, this study examines a corpus of 2,036 articles published across 26 Italian newspapers between 2020 and 2025 to investigate the coverage, newsworthiness criteria, and discursive framing of gang rape. The empirical findings demonstrate a stark discrepancy between press representation and statistical reality: while multi-perpetrator assaults account for approximately 2.06% of recorded rape cases in Italy, they comprise 11.3% of press coverage regarding sexual violence. News coverage is strongly linked to issue continuity, while two primary levers drive case visibility: the elite social status of perpetrators – which lowers news selection thresholds while granting prominent actors platforms to disseminate revictimizing narratives that erase their responsibility– and the intersectional positionality of victims and perpetrators. In cases involving offenders belonging to minoritized groups– more specifically along the axes of oppression of race, migratory status, and social marginality– the press mobilizes femonationalist and securitization rhetorics that conceal male responsibility and attribute GBV to external factors, without questioning fundamental gender power asymmetries. Furthermore, news coverage relies…

items.title: Precision justice in climate adaptation: Diagnosing asymmetric climate risk to target intersectional vulnerability – A Kenyan study with global implications
items.summary_raw: Climate adaptation promises resilience, yet persistent disparities suggest that current investments fail to identify who remains most vulnerable and why. We introduce precision justice - a diagnostic framework centered on asymmetric climate sensitivity that distinguishes households suffering steep yield losses under adverse conditions from those able to benefit under favorable conditions. Applying this framework to 569 maize-producing smallholder households in Western Kenya, we identify a pronounced climate asymmetry trap. Female-headed households in the Lower Midland Zone show the most adverse profile: they exhibit high downside sensitivity and limited relative upside potential, and 57% have yields below the 1.8 t/ha threshold, compared with 0% in more advantaged strata. Their asymmetry ratio – the balance of upside gain to downside loss - is roughly 2.2, less than half that of male-headed households in the same zone. A secondary Rasch-based adoption-propensity measure suggests that implementation capacity may condition some climate-yield relationships, but this evidence is modest and treated as exploratory. These findings challenge universal adaptation models and show how downside-risk diagnostics can inform more precise financial protection, while capacity diagnostics can support better-matched extension. By diagnosing asymmetric risk at the intersection of gender and agroecology, precision justice offers a scalable framework for aligning climate finance with local…

items.title: Mediating Memory: Journalism, Indigenous Knowledge, and the Digital Transformation of Cultural Narratives in Nigeria
items.source_name: RESEARCH JOURNAL OF MASS COMMUNICATION AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY
items.summary_raw: Indigenous knowledge systems (IKS) in Nigeria, rooted in oral traditions, proverbs, rituals, and communal practices, constitute enduring frameworks for cultural memory, environmental knowledge, and social organization. Despite their significance, contemporary journalism operating within data-driven, algorithmic, and digitally accelerated media environments often marginalizes these epistemologies. This paper examines how Nigerian journalism mediates indigenous knowledge in the context of digital transformation shaped by artificial intelligence and information and communication technologies. Using qualitative discourse and framing analysis, the study analyzes selected Nigerian newspapers, broadcast media, and community radio content, alongside indigenous and community-led digital media initiatives. The findings reveal that mainstream journalism frequently frames indigenous knowledge through narratives of cultural loss, nostalgia, and obsolescence, positioning it as residual to scientific and technological knowledge. In contrast, indigenous and alternative media reframe IKS as adaptive, contemporary, and relevant to present-day challenges such as climate adaptation, public health communication, and intergenerational knowledge transmission. The article argues that journalism in Nigeria functions as a critical mediator of cultural memory, shaping epistemic hierarchies by determining which knowledge systems are legitimized, archived, or excluded in public discourse. Drawing on…

items.title: Thawing the climate freeze: a trauma-informed heuristic for collective climate disengagement
items.summary_raw: Climate inaction is often explained by political polarization, material interests, informational deficits, and low perceived efficacy. These accounts are indispensable. Yet they do not fully explain why concern about ecological loss can coexist with emotional numbing and limited sustained engagement. This Perspective advances a trauma-informed heuristic. At the population level, recurring patterns of climate-related avoidance, affective distancing, and routine continuation may be usefully understood as analogous to the protective shutdown and dissociative compartmentalization described in individual trauma theory. This does not imply that societies possess a nervous system, a unified psyche, or a clinical disorder. Rather, the heuristic points to a potentially testable pathway. Through this pathway, threats that are overwhelming, chronic, and difficult to control may narrow emotional processing and perceived agency. This article integrates work on ecological grief, climate distress, collective trauma, and climate communication. It situates these processes alongside the structural and political drivers of inaction. It also identifies community-based, regulation-oriented spaces as promising but unproven candidates for support. Finally, it proposes research priorities. These priorities include operationalizing collective climate disengagement, testing its behavioral correlates, and comparing communication and community interventions that pair accurate threat information with…

items.title: Analysis of the success and failure aspects of cross-border renewable energy powered water desalination plants in conflict zones
items.summary_raw: Cross-border renewable energy powered desalination offers a potential response to water scarcity in conflict-affected regions, but its implementation is constrained by interconnected technical, political, institutional, environmental, financial, and social challenges. This study identifies and prioritizes the critical success factors affecting such projects using the Analytic Hierarchy Process. A multidimensional framework comprising seven main dimensions and 58 sub-criteria was evaluated through structured expert judgments. The results show a balanced distribution among the seven main dimensions, with weights ranging from 0.136 for social and community aspects to 0.146 for environmental and ecological aspects, indicating that no single dimension independently determines project success. At the sub-criterion level, the five highest global weights were obtained for the reliability and efficiency of desalination technology (0.0221), the use of renewable energy to reduce carbon emissions (0.0210), technical compatibility between participating countries’ infrastructure (0.0207), perceived fairness in benefit allocation (0.0203), and clarity of legal frameworks (0.0203). Under a +20% perturbation of each main-criterion weight, 5–7 of the original top ten sub-criteria remained in the top ten, demonstrating reasonable ranking stability. The findings indicate that successful cross-border desalination requires an integrated socio-technical approach combining operational reliability…

items.title: Fossil fuel subsidies prohibitions in the 2024 agreement on climate change, trade and sustainability (ACCTS): an international investment law perspective
items.summary_raw: The 2024 Agreement on Climate Change, Trade and Sustainability (ACCTS), signed by Costa Rica, Iceland, New Zealand, and Switzerland, is the first legally binding international agreement containing fossil fuel subsidy (FFS) prohibitions. At the same time, as the ACCTS operates within an entrenched international economic law framework, there exist important questions concerning the compatibility of FFS prohibitions with existing legal regimes, including international investment law (IIL). This article explores this interaction. It first outlines the scope of ACCTS FFS prohibitions. While the ACCTS attempts to discipline a wide range of subsidies, it also contains various limitations and carve-outs, thus reducing its potential impact. The article then analyses possible legal tensions between FFS reforms and existing IIL obligations of States (fair and equitable treatment, indirect expropriation, national treatment, and most-favored-nation), and examines the potential for investor–state dispute settlement (ISDS) proceedings to arise out of FFS reform efforts. The analysis uses two strands of ISDS jurisprudence, the first involving the fossil fuel industry, and the second concerning subsidy-related disputes, to highlight the potential for IIL to constrain States’ regulatory autonomy concerning FFS reform. The research finds that the four ACCTS Members face limited exposure due to limited investment treaty networks and low levels of subsidization, but also that broader…

items.title: Out of breath, out of mind: Competing frames and public support for carbon taxation in Spain
items.summary_raw: Efforts to implement climate policies often face public resistance. This study, based on a pre-registered survey experiment in Spain, tests how different framings of carbon taxation, emphasizing costs, primary climate benefits, co-benefits, and their combinations, shape public support. Compared to a baseline with no additional information, cost-focused messages reduce support, while benefit frames increase it; co-benefits (cleaner air, better health) produce the largest increase, though in isolation this is not statistically distinguishable from the primary-benefit frame. When paired with cost information, co-benefit framing sustains support more effectively than primary climate benefits, suggesting that immediate, tangible outcomes resonate more strongly with the public than distant climate goals. A dictionary-based analysis of open-ended responses corroborates this interpretation: co-benefit and cost treatments activate frame-aligned language, whereas the primary benefits treatment does not. The study further reveals systematic heterogeneity in responses: cost information reduces support most among left-leaning and lower-income respondents, while co-benefit framing is more persuasive among center- and right-leaning and higher-income respondents. Together, these findings point to a modest but systematic role of framing in shaping attitudes toward carbon taxation, with implications for designing more publicly acceptable climate policies.

items.title: Causal Linkages Between Forestation, Health Issues, and Sustainability Dimensions in the United States and China: A Climate Resilience Perspective
items.summary_raw: ABSTRACT Growing environmental pressures and climate‐related risks have intensified concerns regarding population health and sustainability. This study explores how the predictive relationship between public health and key sustainability indicators, such as agricultural emissions, forests, governance, digitalization, green energy, and climate outcomes, varies over time across the United States and China. For this, the study applied the Bootstrap rolling window Granger causality framework to identify whether health sustainability relationships remain stable or vary over time. The study uses the annual data from 1996 to 2023. The findings revealed different structural patterns. For instance, in the United States, causal flows from sustainability factors to health with episodic positive effects from forest, green energy, and climate outcomes, while digitalization exhibited weak health reinforcement. In contrast, for China, health exhibits stronger predictive effects on agricultural emissions, renewable energy transitions, and governance indicators. The results indicate distinct sustainability health pathways, with environmental conditions playing a more prominent role in health dynamics in the United States, while improvements in health are more closely associated with sustainability transition in China, which can be used to inform resilience‐oriented policy development.

items.title: Advancing climate and health policies in Kenya: Insights from national policy stakeholders
items.source_name: The Journal of Climate Change and Health
items.summary_raw: Introduction Climate change is increasingly recognized as one of the most critical determinants of global public health. The intersection of climate and health requires urgent attention if the impacts of climate change on health are to be mitigated . Kenya has been scaling efforts to address the challenges of the climate-health nexus, but the question of how to integrate climate change and health policy remains unanswered. Materials and methods This study aimed to answer this question by conducting interviews with 21 high-level stakeholders working on climate change, health, and related policy areas in the months of April to July 2024. Data gathered from the interviews was supplemented by climate change and health literature. Results Nearly all respondents agree that climate change and health policy should be explicitly integrated. This integration could enhance the use of financial resources, amplify co-benefits, and simplify the management of the two issues. Integration is, however, barred by the siloed nature of working and limited collaboration within these sectors, limited funding and data access, a shortage of skilled personnel, lack of political goodwill, and weak institutionalization of innovative ideas. To encourage integration, respondents identified interventions such as increased advocacy, public awareness campaigns, and international efforts focused on climate and health solutions. For improved collaboration, several suggestions including establishing…

items.title: Does climate policy kill jobs? Assessing the gap between the measured and perceived job transition risk in Western Canada
items.summary_raw: Compulsory climate policies, including carbon taxes and regulations, have been framed in terms of threats to employment. The ‘job-killing’ narrative has been particularly strong in Canada, where economic concerns have been tied to the consumer carbon tax, leading to its elimination in April 2025. Using a representative web-based survey of communities with fossil fuel-dependent employment in Western Canada (n = 1665), our study aims to: (1) introduce and validate an empirical measure of the perceptions gap between perceived and measured job risk from climate policy, (2) identify the socio-economic, political, and regional determinants of the perceptions gap, and (3) assess how measured risk, perceived risk, and the perceptions gap are associated with support for specific climate policies. We find that perceived and measured job risk are positively correlated, but respondents systematically overestimate risk. Perceived job risk is highest in oil- and gas-producing Alberta, Saskatchewan, and northeastern British Columbia. Sectoral emissions intensity is the strongest predictor of perceived risk. The perceptions gap narrows with higher education and trust in scientists, but widens with income insecurity, right-leaning ideology, and especially engagement with climate delay discourses, which has the largest association. Both measured and perceived risk, and the gap between them, reduce support for most climate policies, particularly industry-focused policies. In contrast…

items.title: ‘Digger’ is the year’s big climate movie. This climate reporter hated it.
items.summary_raw: If you scroll down on the list of “ Carbon Majors ,” the 178 producers that are responsible for most of the world’s fossil fuel emissions, you will eventually get to a company called Continental Resources. This firm is ranked around 150, well after giants like Saudi Aramco and ExxonMobil, but it has still produced almost 600 million tons of carbon dioxide since 2005 alone, equivalent to the combined carbon footprint of around 2 million Americans over that same time. The founder of this company is a man named Harold Hamm, the spitting image of an American oil executive — he grew up dirt-poor in Oklahoma and worked his way into fracking riches, but he still speaks with a Southern drawl . He now uses his wealth to influence the government, raising millions of dollars for Republican candidates and funding crusades against green energy . If you squint, the protagonist of Alejandro González Iñárritu’s new film Digger could pass for Hamm, or for the Hamm-like archetype that has bled into the American psyche. The film centers around an oil executive named Digger Rockwell, a Texas-accented plutocrat who has built his father’s wildcat oil company into a global concern with offshore rigs in Greenland and Alaska. As depicted by Tom Cruise, he is the ideal of the Southern businessman-ideologue, partial to monogrammed private jet seats and roaring rants about his own genitalia. Other than making money, his sole concern seems to be the welfare of his white cat Maggie, whom he is trying to…
